title: Anterior cerebral artery embolus: impaired leg function (climbing stairs)
vignette: A 68-year-old man is evaluated for visual loss in the left eye that resolved spontaneously within several hours. The patient has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and ischemic cardiomyopathy. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. Physical examination reveals a left carotid bruit but no neurologic deficits. A carotid duplex ultrasound shows 85% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery, and carotid angiography with stenting is performed. During the procedure, atherosclerotic debris embolize to the artery indicated by the white arrow on a cerebral MR angiogram of the circle of Willis - the vessel that arises from the internal carotid artery and passes anteromedially between the cerebral hemispheres to supply the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes. Which of the following actions is most likely to be impaired in this patient as a result of the embolization?

clues.text: visual loss in the left eye that resolved spontaneously
clues.note: Transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) from carotid atheroemboli establishes the vascular context: an unstable carotid plaque showering debris intracranially.

clues.text: 85% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery
clues.note: A severely stenotic internal carotid artery is the source of the atheroemboli (and the reason for stenting); debris can travel into its intracranial branches.

clues.text: passes anteromedially between the cerebral hemispheres
clues.note: This describes the ANTERIOR cerebral artery - a branch of the internal carotid that courses in the interhemispheric fissure to supply the medial frontal/parietal cortex, which is the LEG/foot area of the homunculus.

whatMatters: The arrowed vessel is the anterior cerebral artery (branches off the ICA, runs anteromedially between the hemispheres). The ACA supplies the MEDIAL frontal and parietal cortex - the leg/foot region of the motor/sensory homunculus. An ACA embolus therefore impairs contralateral LEG function -> climbing stairs. Answer A. Hand/face/speech/swallowing are MCA territory.
strategy: Identify the artery (ACA) from its course, then apply the homunculus: ACA = medial cortex = contralateral LEG/foot (plus micturition/behavior); MCA = lateral cortex = face/hand + language. Climbing stairs uses the legs (ACA). Gripping (hand), whistling (face), speaking (Broca), and swallowing (face/brainstem) are all MCA/lateral functions.

eliminations.label: Gripping - hand (MCA)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hand/finger motor control. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the hand is represented on the LATERAL convexity (MCA territory), not the medial ACA territory. ✅ Correct if: middle cerebral artery occlusion.

eliminations.label: Speaking - language (MCA, dominant)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: expressive speech (Broca area) in the dominant frontal lobe. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: Broca area is supplied by the MCA, not the ACA. ✅ Correct if: dominant MCA stroke (Broca aphasia).

eliminations.label: Swallowing food - oropharyngeal (MCA/brainstem)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the oropharyngeal/face representation controlling swallowing. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: face/throat map to the LATERAL cortex (MCA) or brainstem, not the ACA. ✅ Correct if: MCA or brainstem lesion causing dysphagia.

eliminations.label: Whistling - face (MCA)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: facial (lip) motor control. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the face lies on the lateral cortex (MCA territory), not the medial ACA territory. ✅ Correct if: MCA occlusion with facial weakness.

reasoning: Carotid atheroemboli during stenting travel into an intracranial branch
The arrowed artery courses anteromedially between the hemispheres = anterior cerebral artery
The ACA supplies the medial cortex = leg/foot area of the homunculus
-> contralateral leg weakness impairs climbing stairs; answer A
mechanism: The anterior cerebral artery arises from the internal carotid artery and courses anteromedially in the interhemispheric fissure to supply the MEDIAL surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes - the cortical territory of the contralateral lower extremity (leg and foot) on the motor and sensory homunculus, along with the frontal micturition center and behavioral areas. Atheroembolic occlusion of the ACA therefore produces contralateral leg/foot weakness and sensory loss (impairing actions such as climbing stairs), and can cause urinary incontinence and abulia. The middle cerebral artery supplies the LATERAL convexity - the face and hand motor/sensory cortex plus, in the dominant hemisphere, language areas - so hand gripping, facial movement (whistling), speech, and swallowing map to MCA rather than ACA territory.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Neuro > ACA vs MCA territories and the motor/sensory homunculus; circle of Willis; amaurosis fugax from carotid disease.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Chain: identify the artery (ACA) -> its cortical territory (medial = leg) -> the impaired action (climbing stairs).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on homunculus, amaurosis fugax, anteromedial, abulia, or interhemispheric fissure? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Hand (gripping), face (whistling), speech, and swallowing are all MCA/lateral functions - tempting because they're motor tasks, but they aren't ACA territory.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On the MRA, find the artery that branches off the internal carotid and runs forward/medially between the hemispheres = ACA. Anchor: 'medial midline artery = ACA = leg.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: ACA = medial cortex = contralateral LEG (+/- incontinence, abulia); MCA = lateral cortex = face/hand + language.

keywords.back: Contralateral LEG/foot weakness + sensory loss (+/- incontinence, abulia)

keywords.front: Artery off the ICA coursing anteromedially between hemispheres

keywords.back: Transient monocular vision loss from carotid atheroemboli

firstAid.detail: Neuro: ACA -> contralateral leg > arm weakness; medial cortex/homunculus; micturition/abulia.
firstAid.location: Neuro: ACA -> contralateral leg > arm weakness; medial cortex/homunculus; micturition/abulia.

firstAid.detail: Neuro > MCA -> face/arm weakness, aphasia (dominant), neglect (nondominant).
firstAid.location: Neuro > MCA -> face/arm weakness, aphasia (dominant), neglect (nondominant).

firstAid.detail: Neuro > circle of Willis; carotid atheroemboli -> amaurosis fugax / stroke; endarterectomy/stenting.
firstAid.location: Neuro > circle of Willis; carotid atheroemboli -> amaurosis fugax / stroke; endarterectomy/stenting.

memoryHook: ACA feeds the medial strip - the LEG lives there. Embolus to the ACA = can't climb stairs; the hand and face belong to the MCA.
